entries.complaint: "Runs the original EPANET solver" -- "original" reads two ways: the authentic/actual EPANET program, or the FIRST VERSION of it as opposed to a later one. A translator with no other context is as likely to pick the version reading, which would be false.
readings: the first/earliest version of the EPANET solver (false)
entries.resolution: Rewritten to "Runs EPANET's own solver from the US EPA". Possessive states authenticity without the version ambiguity, and it contrasts cleanly with "the built-in solver" in the next sentence.

entries.complaint: English source changed from "EPANET Engine" to "EPANET Solver" (Tom, 2026-08-13). Romance languages had rendered "engine" as motor/moteur/motore -- correct for software, but this calculator models PUMPS, where a motor is a physical component, so the software sense collides with a hydraulic one on the same page.
readings: a physical motor, as on a pump (the collision)
entries.resolution: All five 'engine' keys changed to 'solver' in English, which also matches the page's own long-standing 'built-in solver' wording. Russian had already avoided the trap independently with расчётным ядром (computational core), and Portuguese had split against itself (Motor EPANET in the title, mecanismo do EPANET in the setting) -- both signs the English word was the problem. Resynced across 26 languages as sprint 252.

entries.complaint: The English uses two different phrasings for the same concept ("EPANET's own solver" vs "the built-in solver"), which invites drifting onto two different nouns in Russian even though both must read as the same kind of thing for the contrast to work.
readings: one noun for both, qualifier carries the difference (chosen)
two nouns, mirroring the English word variation
entries.resolution: Valid and important -- the agent found the general rule from one string. The English variation is possessive-vs-adjective ('EPANET's own' / 'the built-in'), not two different nouns; both are 'solver'. But the risk it names is real and was realised in 20+ languages BEFORE this sprint, which is exactly how the defect got in. Answered in the new glossary term 'solver': use ONE noun for both and let the qualifier carry the difference. The ru agent also found its own file had drifted onto решатель vs ядро and standardized, fixing a gender agreement as a consequence. No English change: the variation reads naturally to an English reader and carries the intended emphasis.

entries.complaint: The pre-existing Indonesian used a different word (mesin) for the identical concept than the built-in-solver string (penyelesai) already used, so the resync was not only an English-follows edit but also fixed a same-page terminology inconsistency predating this sprint.
readings: treat as a terminology bug and fix now (chosen)
leave mesin, since only the English of lpn_main_title literally changed
entries.resolution: Chose correctly, and the observation generalises further than the agent could see from inside one language: the SAME split existed in more than twenty files (sr језгро/решавач, cs jádro/řešič, hi इंजन/सॉल्वर, tr motor/çözücü, ro motorul/rezolvitorul, and so on). That is the signature of an English-source defect reproduced faithfully by good translators, not of 20 independent mistakes -- and it is the strongest evidence for Tom's decision to change the English word rather than guard it. Recorded in the 'solver' glossary entry.
